title: Suggestions for adapting httr2 to work on hosted versions of Posit Workbench
description:
Hi all,
    I noticed an issue in the implementation of the authorization code flow for httr2 that seems to hard-code assumptions for redirects that would only be consistent with running RStudio Workbench on a local laptop. 

I played with using httr2, and wanted to offer some suggestions / adjustments that could help people in my situation, which is operating with a hosted version of Posit Workbench, using a custom identity provider (not google).
    

I pasted the code for the function `httr2:::oauth_flow_auth_code` below. 

```{r}
httr2:::oauth_flow_auth_code

function (client, auth_url, scope = NULL, pkce = TRUE, auth_params = list(), 
    token_params = list(), host_name = "localhost", host_ip = "127.0.0.1", 
    port = httpuv::randomPort()) 
{
    oauth_flow_check("authorization code", client, interactive = TRUE)
    check_installed("httpuv")
    if (pkce) {
        code <- oauth_flow_auth_code_pkce()
        auth_params$code_challenge <- code$challenge
        auth_params$code_challenge_method <- code$method
        token_params$code_verifier <- code$verifier
    }
    state <- base64_url_rand(32)
    redirect_url <- paste0("http://", host_name, ":", port, "/")  # Point #1
    user_url <- oauth_flow_auth_code_url(client, auth_url = auth_url, 
        redirect_uri = redirect_url, scope = scope, state = state, 
        auth_params = auth_params)
    utils::browseURL(user_url) ## point #2
    result <- oauth_flow_auth_code_listen(host_ip, port)  ## point #2
    code <- oauth_flow_auth_code_parse(result, state)
    oauth_client_get_token(client, grant_type = "authorization_code", 
        code = code, redirect_uri = redirect_url, !!!token_params)
}

```

If you take a look at the code, the first concern for me was that the redirect_url is being built from the following line:

redirect_url <- paste0("http://", host_name, ":", port, "/")

This line is designed to work for a localhost redirect, but not well suited for a hosted R Workbench session. In my organization the redirect url needs to be SSL secured, but there is not an option to use https.

Additionally, the redirect in this case may be a website (for example hosted in Posit Connect), which means that there is no port number.

My suggestion is to make the redirect url a parameter and default it to a function like:
```{r}
build_localhost_redirect_url = function(host_ip, port, secure_protocol){
   if(secure_protocol) protocol = "https" else protocol = "http"
   paste0(protocol, "://", host_name, ":", port, "/")
}
```
In this way, I can choose to pass a custom url, or use the function to generate my local redirect url as needed.

The next issue is that the "listening" for a code makes a hard assumption that the user is on their local PC, with access to localhost, using the code snippet below.
```{r}
    utils::browseURL(user_url) ## point #2
    result <- oauth_flow_auth_code_listen(host_ip, port)  ## point #2
```

My suggestion is that there is another argument, such as local = TRUE, which would select between the use of `httr2:::oauth_flow_auth_code_listen`

or using the` oauth_exchanger` function from httr. 

The `httr::oauth_exchanger` lets you paste in the code that you receive manually, which is needed when authenticating on a remote server (such as the hosted Posit Workbench.)

```{r}
httr:::oauth_exchanger = function (request_url) 
{
    BROWSE(request_url)
    authorization_code <- str_trim(readline("Enter authorization code: "))
    list(code = authorization_code)
}
```

Alternatively you could maybe pass in your own function? In any case, being able to just paste in the code from the redirect url manually would be a big plus for those working in a hosted version of Workbench.

Another question / adaptation I would request is to make/add more functions/documentation around saving the tokens from the authorization flow.

For my use case, I wanted to use the auth_code approach with a stored token. However, I initially couldn't figure out how to do this. Some search of the functions led me to realize that what I wanted was to utilize the 

`httr2::req_oauth_auth_code` function, instead of manually getting the token and saving it. I had a hard time figuring out that I needed this function and how to break down the process of token retrieving / storing. 

I was able to figure it out by going through all the functions and seeing exactly where tokens were generated/stored, but I thought this could use more documentation. 
   
```{r}

httr2::req_oauth_auth_code = function (req, client, auth_url, cache_disk = FALSE, cache_key = NULL, 
    scope = NULL, pkce = TRUE, auth_params = list(), token_params = list(), 
    host_name = "localhost", host_ip = "127.0.0.1", port = httpuv::randomPort()) 
{
    params <- list(client = client, auth_url = auth_url, scope = scope, 
        pkce = pkce, auth_params = auth_params, token_params = token_params, 
        host_name = host_name, host_ip = host_ip, port = port)
    cache <- cache_choose(client, cache_disk, cache_key)
    req_oauth(req, "oauth_flow_auth_code", params, cache = cache)
}

```

I can see that the `cache_choose` function is used to define the cache, and store it to the disk. This makes sense. But then, the req_oauth function is expecting the cache, which is passed as an argument to req_policies.

Going further down the rabbit hole I was confused about how to actually build this on my own. 

I ended up using the exact same structure as req_oauth, and passing my custom function for getting a token to req_oauth (get_lea_token).  

If you could add documentation and examples about how to properly

1) store tokens to disk for later use
2) The fact that tokens are stored as .Rds files (I didnt know that and it wasnt obvious at first)
3) How to better customize the save location for tokens.

That would be awesome.

Here is the example of my function.

```{r}
req_oauth_auth_code_lea = function(req)
{
  client = make_lea_client()
  cache_disk = TRUE
  cache_key = NULL
  params <- list(client = client)
  cache <- httr2:::cache_choose(client, cache_disk, cache_key)
  httr2:::req_oauth(req, "get_lea_token", params, cache = cache)
}
```

For point #3 above, I thought it may be worthwhile to have the app_path be an argument to the cache_disk function, so that I can customize it to save into a different cache location. It isn't a huge deal, but I was initially confused by the fact that "httr2" was hard coded into the path.

```{r}
httr2:::cache_disk = function (client, key) 
{
    app_path <- file.path(rappdirs::user_cache_dir("httr2"), 
        client$name)
    dir.create(app_path, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
    path <- file.path(app_path, paste0(hash(key), "-token.rds.enc"))
    list(get = function() if (file.exists(path)) secret_read_rds(path, 
        obfuscate_key()) else NULL, set = function(token) secret_write_rds(token, 
        path, obfuscate_key()), clear = function() if (file.exists(path)) file.remove(path))
}
```
 
Finally, I initially had some trouble with capturing the oauth redirect code from the URL, and did not understand how to deploy a site to do this capture on our internal system.

The gargle repository provides an example html site (https://github.com/r-lib/gargle/blob/main/inst/pseudo-oob/google-callback/index.html) that one could use, but I didn't immediately understand what the site was doing. This is mainly because I am not good with html/css.

So I was facing two challenges. 1) How to deploy a site and 2) Needing to understand what the html was doing.

After talking with Jenny Bryan (thanks!!), I understand what the html in the demo was doing that was causing issues with the code capture. There was a conversion to a JSON in the code, which I did not know how to deal with.

In any case, I was able to deploy the site to Posit Connect by using a R Markdown document with the following code:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
htmltools::includeHTML("gargle_page.html")
```

I don't know if this is the best, but I didn't know how else to (quickly) deploy a piece of custom html.


However, I think an R-focused approach would be best to let R users better understand the exact workflow of the redirect capture. I thought a shiny app deployed on Posit Connect would be the easiest way to approach the problem for me.


The code below was adapted from this stack overflow example https://community.rstudio.com/t/getting-url-parameters-in-a-shiny-dashboard-app/35611/3 (thanks!).

I thought that this shiny example could be integrated into the code base for httr2, so that someone could tweak it, and deploy to a server like Posit Connect with a single click.

```{r}
library(shiny)
library(shinydashboard)
library(rclipboard)

ui <- bootstrapPage(
  rclipboardSetup(),
    h3("Here is your Dow Token"),
    verbatimTextOutput("queryText"),

    # UI ouputs for the copy-to-clipboard buttons
    uiOutput("clip"),
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
 
  code = reactive({
    query <- parseQueryString(session$clientData$url_search)
    query$code
    })
  
  output$queryText <- renderText({
    code()
  })
  
  output$clip <- renderUI({
    rclipButton(
      inputId = "clipbtn",
      label = "Click to copy the code!",
      clipText = code(), 
      icon = icon("clipboard")
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

```


I was able to deploy this code on our Connect instance and have the administrators add the custom assigned url to the list of allowed redirects. That solved the problem and I was able to get the custom oauth to work.

Let me know if these suggestions are helpful, or if you need any other code examples.

title: Diferent refresh token in each oauth refresh
description:
In #122 it was mentioned how to set the token with an access and a refresh token in the Twitter API.

httr2 has a `oauth_flow_refresh` (which is not in the reference page in the website) to refresh an access token if needed has expired. It checks that the new refresh token is the same as the previous one. However, Twitter doesn't use the same refresh token always, each time [the refresh token changes](https://twittercommunity.com/t/unable-to-obtain-new-access-token-by-using-refresh-token/164123/16). This is related to #186 if not the same issue.

Using `oauth_flow_refresh` expires the current token because the refresh token is used but an error is triggered without returning the new token. 

I would suggest a new parameter `strict = TRUE` to control if the check of the new refresh token is different from the old one. This would be backwards compatible and would work in this scenario by setting a `strict = FALSE`.

title: Introduce an `append = TRUE` option to `req_body_json`
description:
In situations where one is going to loop through multiple pages, it would be useful to preserve the original body, but be able to add to it, such as `page = 2`... etc: 

```R
library(httr2)

token = "my_token"

# Set up the original request

url = "https://api.mavenlink.com/api/v1/custom_field_values"
req = request(url) |>
  req_method('GET') |>
  req_headers() |>
  req_body_json(
    list(subject_type = 'Workspace',
         per_page = 200)
  ) |> 
  req_auth_bearer_token(token)


# We can only have 200 pages at a time, so we need to loop and add to results
results = list()

# Get the first 200 Rows
resp = req |>
  req_perform()

# Pull out the data
data = resp |>
  resp_body_json()

# Check if there is more data, and get the next starting point
total_pages = data$meta$page_count


current_page = data$meta$page_number

has_more = current_page < total_pages
next_page = current_page + 1

# Save the data
results = c(results, data |> pluck('custom_field_values'))


# Now loop until we have all the data
while (has_more) {
  
  resp = req |>
    # Add an argument to start where we left off on the last loop. 
    
    # Here's the issue: if I only provide page, I loose 
    # the subject type, and per_page arguments specified above. 
    # If I respecify them, its not DRY
    req_body_json(
      list(page = next_page,
           subject_type = 'Workspace',
           per_page = 200
      )) |>
    req_perform()
  
  data = resp |>
    resp_body_json()
  
  results = c(results, data |> pluck('custom_field_values'))
  
  current_page = data$meta$page_number
  has_more = current_page < total_pages
  next_page = current_page + 1
}
```

what would be awesome is to do `req_body_json(page = next_page, append=TRUE)` to preserve the previously specified arguments.

When I was trying to figure out why my redirects work with `httr` but not with `httr2`, I saw that `httr::POST()` includes `_nss=1` by default. title: Trouble using streaming data and WebSocket with httr2
description:
I'm writing a API wrapper package using `httr2` and have an issue with streaming data. I'm not sure if this is a bug or the functionality is just not covered by `httr2`.

My use case is to get stock prices from a streaming endpoint, using the common workflow of creating a subscriprtion, then receiving streams of data from that subscription. 

My provider is [Saxo Bank](https://www.developer.saxo/openapi/learn), their API documentation for streams is [here](https://www.developer.saxo/openapi/learn/streaming), whith [this](https://www.developer.saxo/openapi/learn/streaming#:~:text=let%20us%20know.-,Connecting%20to%20the%20WebSocket%20server,-To%20connect%20to) section being the most relevant. 

The idea is to send a GET request to an endpoint, including a `contextId`. With headers `Connection: Upgrade` and `Upgrade: WebSocket`, the connection upgrades to the WebSocket protocol, `wss://`. However, I don't seem to recieve any streaming data, and I can't figure out if it is because WebSocket is not supported, if there's a bug, or if I'm doing something wrong. Below is a code snippet to show what I'm doing. 

Any help much appreciated. 

Code:

```
# Try handling streaming responses from Saxo with httr2

library(tidyverse)
library(httr2)

# 24 hour token for simulation environment
token24  <- "BEARER [TOKEN]"

# Create subscription for a specific stock
req <-
  request("https://gateway.saxobank.com/sim/openapi/trade/v1/prices/subscriptions") %>%
  req_body_json(data = list(
    "Arguments" =
      list("Uic" = 15611,
           "AssetType" = "Stock"),
    "ContextId" = "aUv1j3U-Or3", # Arbitrary string, for identification
    "ReferenceId" = "5MolAro8Zz")) %>%
  req_headers(Authorization = token24)

resp_status_desc(r) # "Created" -- works nicely so far

# Streaming responses
# First, a call-back function
write_stream <- function(x) {
  x %>% write_file("data-raw/temp", append = TRUE)
  TRUE
}

# Make GET request, as explained here:
# https://www.developer.saxo/openapi/learn/streaming#:~:text=let%20us%20know.-,Connecting%20to%20the%20WebSocket%20server,-To%20connect%20to

req <- request("https://streaming.saxobank.com/sim/openapi/streamingws/connect") %>%
  req_url_query(`contextId`= "aUv1j3U-Or3") %>%
  req_headers(Authorization = token24,
              Connection = "Upgrade",
              Upgrade = "Websocket",
              `Sec-WebSocket-Key` = "SGVsbG8sIHdvcmxkIQ==",
              `Sec-WebSocket-Version` = 13)

req %>% req_stream(write_stream) # Nothing happens
```

title: OAuth caching does not respect `refresh_token`
description:
The caching does not respect the refresh token.

``` r
library(httr2)

client <- oauth_client("example", "https://example.com/get_token")
req <- request("https://example.com")

# create 2 requests with different refresh token
req1 <- req %>% 
  req_oauth_refresh(client, refresh_token = "rt1")
req2 <- req %>% 
  req_oauth_refresh(client, refresh_token = "rt2")

# simulate that we made a request and got back a token
token <- oauth_token(
  access_token = "a",
  token_type = "bearer",
  expires_in = NULL,
  refresh_token = "rt1",
  .date = Sys.time()
)
# ... that is now cached
req1$policies$auth_oauth$cache$set(token)
req1$policies$auth_oauth$cache$get() %>% str()
#> List of 3
#>  $ token_type   : chr "bearer"
#>  $ access_token : chr "a"
#>  $ refresh_token: chr "rt1"
#>  - attr(*, "class")= chr "httr2_token"
# but also in req2
req2$policies$auth_oauth$cache$get() %>% str()
#> List of 3
#>  $ token_type   : chr "bearer"
#>  $ access_token : chr "a"
#>  $ refresh_token: chr "rt1"
#>  - attr(*, "class")= chr "httr2_token"

# or shown in `auth_oauth_sign()` which is used in `req_perform()`
req1 %>% 
  httr2:::auth_oauth_sign() %>% 
  print(redact_headers = FALSE)
#> <httr2_request>
#> GET https://example.com
#> Headers:
#> • Authorization: 'Bearer a'
#> Body: empty
#> Policies:
#> • auth_oauth: a list

req2 %>% 
  httr2:::auth_oauth_sign() %>% 
  print(redact_headers = FALSE)
#> <httr2_request>
#> GET https://example.com
#> Headers:
#> • Authorization: 'Bearer a'
#> Body: empty

```

title: Discussion on expanding `httr2::oauth_client()`
description:
This isn't really an issue, but really a discussion to collect thoughts on how I'm currently defining and using an OAuth2 client object for an API wrapper package, and whether it might form the basis of a new article.

I originally had the code of my client package using particular settings in terms of how it interfaced with the API baked in (hardcoded) to a lot of the functions. After reading in the Wrapping APIs vignette "you should always provide some way for the user to provide their own app", I thought about how I might separate out this logic to make it easier for a developer/user to change.

I've ended up creating a function which wraps `httr2::oauth_client()` but also adorns the object with additional client settings in terms of how it interfaces with the API.

```
my_client <- function(client_name = "My API client",
                       client_id = "44es4rere",
                       client_secret = httr2::obfuscated("fgesg5r4ste"),
                       store_token_on_disk = TRUE,
                       host = "http://sitename",
                       user_agent = "My API client (me@domain.com)",
                       req_rate = 1/3,
                       max_tries = 2){
  
  cl <- httr2::oauth_client(id = client_id,
                            token_url = paste(host, "oauth2", "token", sep = "/"),
                            secret = client_secret,
                            auth = "header",
                            name = client_name)
  
  cl$auth_url = paste(host, "oauth2", "authorize", sep = "/")
  cl$store_token_on_disk <- store_token_on_disk
  cl$host <- host
  cl$user_agent <- user_agent
  cl$req_rate <- req_rate
  cl$max_tries <- max_tries
  cl
}
```

All of my top level function then take in a client object with `my_client()` being the default.

Obviously you could customise this based on which `httr2` features you've chosen to use; I've not chosen to use an explicit backoff for example. This obviates the need for me to have lots of these parameters floating around as function arguments and I can just store them in one object which characterises the client's interface to the API. I like it because everything is defined in one place.

My ultimate question is whether this is a sensible way of doing things and if anyone has done something similar? If it is of use, I wonder if it is something to write about in a article/vignette?

title: Duplicated client entries on authorised apps list
description:
I'm writing a client for the Jive API using the oauth_auth_code flow and it my code looks something like this:

```
cl <- httr2::oauth_client(id = "djwniduwdniwudqi.i",
                            token_url = token_url,
                            secret = httr2::obfuscated("erfw8f473h8wu4"),

    httr2::req_oauth_auth_code(cl,

title: possibly add a function to modify curl handle options
description:
First of all, thanks for this package! 

I wonder if it is possible to have a function to control curl handle options? I noticed that [`req_perform` function](https://github.com/r-lib/httr2/blob/main/R/req-perform.R#L294) will eventually set the handle options using the `req$options` but there are only several items can be modified by the existing functions (useragent, proxy, etc). If, for example, I want to set the `maxage_conn` option, I have to do:

```
req <- request("https://example.com") %>% 
  req_proxy("127.0.0.1", 1234) %>% 
  req_user_agent("something here")
req$options$maxage_conn <- 10
```

I was thinking if it is better to have a similar `httr2-style` function, say `req_curl_options = function(.req, ...)`, to directly modify the content of the request options? Thus, the request can be chained in the usual way:

```
req <- request("https://example.com") %>% 
  req_proxy("127.0.0.1", 1234) %>% 
  req_user_agent("something here") %>% 
  req_curl_options(maxage_conn = 10) # not implemented, just concept
```

title: Problems with Device Code + PKCE authentication on remote machines
description:
Hi all,

I had made some contributions to the device code authentication with PKCE in the past and we have used it as our main authentication procedure, which works under normal circumstances (local client) perfectly fine.

Recently, we have setup up a Jupyter notebook with an R Kernel on a remote server. That's where the problem begins. The Jupyter  environment is regarded as an interactive session `rlang::is_interactive()` and httr2 tries to open up the internet browser that is defined in Rs global environment. Unfortunetly the user never gets to see the browser, because it gets executed on the remote machine. And usually you would expect that the URL and the code is printed to console in order to open the browser on your local machine, as it is already defined [here](https://github.com/r-lib/httr2/blob/487c23e203e38539198432c025fc16b48bf2d498/R/oauth-flow-device.R#L85).

Our workaround for this in the Jupyter notebook would be to run the authentication in a temporary non-interactive state with  `rlang::with_interactive({...}, value=FALSE)`. This way we keep the general interactiveness of Jupyter and disable it once during authentication. So far, so good.

Now, there is still a big issue with this approach. [This line](https://github.com/r-lib/httr2/blob/487c23e203e38539198432c025fc16b48bf2d498/R/oauth-flow-device.R#L61) is blocking this non-interactive state. As I understand, the intention for `oauth_flow_check(...,interactive=TRUE)` is a legacy thing, that is was assumed that the user needs to be actively involved by direct interaction with the browser. To cut it short, this line throws an error, because this "interactive state" is required and prevents the printing of the URL and the code from ever being called. 

My question is whether the `oauth_flow_check` is really required here or the default value for `interactive` could be changed to `rlang::is_interactive()`?

Best regards,
Florian

httr2::oauth_flow_auth_code(client,

```
api_request_function <- function(client) {
  httr2::request("[MY_API_URL]") |>
    httr2::req_url_path_append("[PATH_ONE]") |>
    httr2::req_url_path_append("[PATH_TWO]") |>
    httr2::req_oauth_client_credentials(

title: Escaping ascii characters in queries
description:
:wave: Thanks for your continued work on this. Love the "lazy" nature of httr2 v httr

When httr2 is passed a collapsed string of query parameters it automatically escapes then which seems sensible:

``` r
library(httr2)
req <- request("http://example.com")

# Change url components
two_queries <- c("one", "two")
collapsed_query <- paste0(two_queries, collapse = ",")

## automatically converts , to %2
(req <- req %>%
  req_url_query(q = collapsed_query))
#> <httr2_request>
#> GET http://example.com?q=one%2Ctwo
#> Body: empty
```
In {httr} there was, however, the option of unescaping that using `I`:

```r
library(httr)
r <- GET("http://example.com",
  query = list(q = I(collapsed_query))
)

## can use I to use as is
r$url
#> [1] "http://example.com/?q=one,two"
```

This does not work in {httr2}. In {httr} this is accomplished via:
https://github.com/r-lib/httr/blob/21ff69f219ad11298854a63b8f753389088cf382/R/url-query.r#L25-L28

So unless I am missing something (which is of course possible!) we are stuck with doing stuff like:

```r
req <- req %>%
  req_url_query(q = collapsed_query)
req$url <- curl::curl_unescape(req$url)
req
#> <httr2_request>
#> GET http://example.com?q=one,two
#> Body: empty
```

Would you be amenable to a PR that added an `escape`-like function somewhere, probably in httr2:::url_build`?

title: Windows authentication (Kerberos/NTLM)
description:
In `httr` you're able to work with Windows authentication (Kerberos/NTLM) by providing the following object in the GET request:

Is it possible to do this with `httr2`? The recent implementation of `req_proxy()` seems to use some of the same infrastructure, but there's no proxy URL that needs to be defined.

title: More glue-like behavior for `req_template()`
description:
I was surprised to see the following behavior. While everything works nicely in the first example, things fall apart as soon as eval is required. Of course, this can easily be avoided, I just thought I'd point it out as it caught me off guard, given the glue-like syntax.

```r
library(httr2)

req <- request("http://httpbin.org/cookies")

name <- "id"
value <- "a3fWa"

req_template(req, "GET /set/{name}/{value}")
#> <httr2_request>
#> GET http://httpbin.org/cookies/set/id/a3fWa
#> Body: empty

lst <- list(name = "id")
fun <- function() "a3fWa"

req_template(req, "GET /set/{lst$name}/{lst$value}")
#> <httr2_request>
#> GET http://httpbin.org/cookies/set/{lst$name}/{fun()}
#> Body: empty
```

title: Make `req_template()` append the path, instead of replace
description:
It is somewhat inconvenient that when modifying an existing request, the path gets overwritten wholly. Using `req_url_path_append()` instead of `req_url_path()` would be more convenient. For example, the MediaWiki REST API has a path component which is common for all endpoints, but it gets overwritten if I use `req_template()`.

Could we squeeze this in for 0.2, if it makes sense?

title: Unable to handle req_stream errors due to stream open throwing an error
description:
I'm writing an API wrapper that POSTs a command to the server via req_stream to select which data to return. If the posted body is malformed, the server responds with error code 400 causing the open command within req_stream to throw an error. The error prevents the subsequent reading of the error contents by the callback and prevents the subsequent creation of a new_response return value containing the status code.

The R curl_fetch_stream function does not suffer this same limitation because it opens the stream using "rbf" mode instead of "rb" mode. According to the curl's internal code comment, "# 'f' means: do not error for status code".

I request that req_stream be modified such that

stream <- curl::curl(req$url, handle = handle)
open(stream, "rb")

becomes

stream <- curl::curl(req$url, handle = handle)
open(stream, "rbf")

My local testing shows that this change prevents R from throwing an error, allows subsequent parsing of the stream contents, and correctly creates the new_response code with the observed status code.

title: `req_oauth_password` requests passwords regardless of cached token
description:
After reading the documentation, I understand that the various OAuth flows are supposed to get a token and cache it so that a user doesn't have to keep authorizing themselves. I have some code which looks similar to this (I've copied and pasted from the vignette and changed a bit for illustrative purposes):

```
request("https://api.github.com/user") %>% 
  req_oauth_password(client, username = "user", cache_disk = TRUE) %>% 
  req_perform() %>% 
  resp_body_json()
```

If I then perform another request by using the same code above but changing the url in the request call, it requests my password again, even though a token has already been stored. Based on what I've read in the docs, I expected the `req_oauth_password()` call to check for a cached token before asking for my password again. Am I misreading the docs or fundamentally misunderstanding how these functions are supposed to be used? I would have imagined I would need to keep calling the `req_oauth_password()` for each request just in case the token had expired and needed to be refreshed.

title: Questions about secret management
description:
Thanks for the this new incarnation of `{httr}`! I had used `{httr}` before,  and it was really helpful but now `{httr2}` is even better :)

I had written a few API wrappers in the past, but all were accessing public web APIs and there was no need for authentication. Now I'm trying to write my first wrapper using authentication with `{httr2}`. I just read the vignette [Wrapping APIs](https://httr2.r-lib.org/articles/wrapping-apis.html) and I have one question about secret management. I hope you may clarify.

Under [Secret Management](https://httr2.r-lib.org/articles/wrapping-apis.html#secret-management) section, you start by introducing the `secret_encrypt()`, `secret_decrypt()` and `secret_make_key()` functions as an approach to deal with (encrypted) secrets in the source code. You first toy example is for a putative secret that is needed to work with an API.

Your example seems to suggest that, e.g., an API token, should be passed around in code, encrypted, and that a package key (generated with `secret_make_key()`) should be used to decrypt the token as needed. This package key, in turn, ought to be saved in `.Renviron` and retrieved with `Sys.getenv()` when needed. So my question is: why not save the API token in `.Renviron`, and read it directly from there? Are you purposely avoiding this approach for some security reason?

I had a look at packages listed as Reverse imports of `{httr2}`, and from source code inspection they all seem to read "secrets" needed to authenticate with APIs directly from the `.Renviron`.

So this makes me wonder the case where you would use `secret_encrypt()`, `secret_decrypt()` and `secret_make_key()` functions? Is it because you can have many secrets associated with an API, and that it would not be very practical to create environment variables for all those secrets, and therefore it is best to have them in my source code, encrypted, with the corresponding encryption key stored in `.Renviron`? Or is it somehow related to compliance with external workflows that need to access your secrets?

My question here also applies to your example of `get_api_key()` that handles the `{testthat`} context. Why, again, is in his example the testing key decrypted using `"HTTR2_KEY"`, while the `NYTIMES_KEY` is simply retrieved from the `.Renviron`? Why not retrieve both from `.Renviron`?

And, finally, when you suggest `set_api_key()` function for setting the API key, you mention that it is not good to encourage the user to type their secret into the console. But, then, why provide the example with the `key` argument? Why not simply...

```r
set_api_key <- function() {
  key <- askpass::askpass("Please enter your API key")
  Sys.setenv("NYTIMES_KEY" = key)
}
```

As a suggestion, and for someone who's just starting to deal with secrets and keys, it would be great to have an infographics depicting what is meant by package key, encryption key, secret and token, and the place in the filesystem relative to the package source where all this pieces of info should be.

All this being said, I really liked reading this vignette, and I think it is very clear.

Thanks in advance.

title: In `req_body_json`, top level list elements are treated differently than lower level for NULL and empty values
description:
If our `NULL` or empty list is tucked within a list, we're good:

```r
library(httr2)

url <- "http://httpbin.org/"
req <- request(url)

body <- req |>
    req_body_json(list(a=1, b=list(x=3,y=list()), c=list(x=2, z=NULL))) |>
    req_dry_run()

#> POST / HTTP/1.1
#> Host: httpbin.org
#> User-Agent: httr2/0.1.1 r-curl/4.3.2 libcurl/7.77.0
#> Accept: */*
#> Accept-Encoding: deflate, gzip
#> Content-Type: application/json
#> Content-Length: 47
#> 
#> {"a":1,"b":{"x":3,"y":[]},"c":{"x":2,"z":null}}
```
So `y` gives `[]` and `z` gives `null` (or `{}` if we set `null = "list"`).

However, if these are top-level, they just get eliminated (and setting `null` has no effect):
```r
library(httr2)

url <- "http://httpbin.org/"
req <- request(url)

body <- req |>
    req_body_json(list(y=list(), z=NULL, x=list(a=1, b=2))) |>
    req_dry_run()
#> POST / HTTP/1.1
#> Host: httpbin.org
#> User-Agent: httr2/0.1.1 r-curl/4.3.2 libcurl/7.77.0
#> Accept: */*
#> Accept-Encoding: deflate, gzip
#> Content-Type: application/json
#> Content-Length: 19
#> 
#> {"x":{"a":1,"b":2}}
```

This makes it hard to send an empty array to a REST API that requires it at the top level (or maybe I'm missing something).

This could be similar to https://github.com/r-lib/httr2/issues/95, in that it's because of: https://github.com/r-lib/httr2/blob/87011c0ff31019409c4a5a700b041f279f054361/R/req-body.R#L104

title: `req_body_form()` silently drops duplicate names
description:
In order to POST a form on a website where all the checkboxes have identical names, I need to pass a list with duplicate names. But, the duplicates are silently dropped.

The culprit seems to be `.x[names(dots)] <- dots` in [modify_list()](https://github.com/r-lib/httr2/blob/87011c0ff31019409c4a5a700b041f279f054361/R/utils.R#L31).

It could be replaced with something like

```
.x[names(.x) %in% names(dots)] <- NULL
.x <- c(.x, dots)
```

which would have the advantage of replacing entire homonym groups, and would pass the current tests for `modify_list()`.

It wouldn't help with the headaches in #95 ~and # 88~ though (I am not sure about the # 88).

For a more systematic solution, how about an additional argument `replace = TRUE`, or a dedicated `req_body_form_modify()` so that we can decide whether the body gets replaced instead of combined?

- `req_body_*`: replaces entire body, avoiding the `modify_list()` call
- `req_body_*_modify`: combines lists

title: Stacking queries in req_url_query()
description:
In some APIs, such as for [Jive](https://developers.jivesoftware.com/api/v3/cloud/rest/index.html), you can **stack** query parameters with the same name and differentiate them in the values, however the default behaviour of `httr2` seems to be to overwrite them if they have the same name, e.g.:

`httr2::req_url_query(req, filter = "name(Hadley)", filter = "company(rstudio)")`

Would it be worth adding a parameter to switch off this behaviour?

title: Feature request: additional headers to the requests by oauth_client()
description:
I wanted to try Twitter's API with OAuth2, but this code

``` r
client <- oauth_client(
  id = "<client ID>",
  secret = obfuscated("<obfuscated client secret>"),
  token_url = "https://api.twitter.com/2/oauth2/token",
  name = "rstats_ja_bot_test"
)

token <- oauth_flow_auth_code(client, 
  auth_url = "https://twitter.com/i/oauth2/authorize",
  scope = "tweet.read tweet.write offline.access",
  host_name = "127.0.0.1",
  port = 1410
)
```

ended up with this error:

```
Waiting for authentication in browser...
Press Esc/Ctrl + C to abort
Error in `oauth_flow_abort()`:
! OAuth failure [unauthorized_client]
• Missing valid authorization header
```

After googling with the error message "Missing valid authorization header," I got to know that Twitter OAuth2 API requires a Basic authorization header for OAuth authorization.

https://twittercommunity.com/t/trying-to-get-oauth-2-0-token-receiving-missing-valid-authorization-header-error/163633/4

IIUC, httr2 doesn't provide the argument that the users can use to customize the requests like this. This case might be a rare one, but I'm wondering if there are more cases where the users need low level access.

title: Invalid signature with sha256 encoding
description:
I've been building some API functions that require sha256 encoding for private keys and the code works in httr terminology but what I believe to be the same call fails in httr2.

```r
api.url <- "https://api.pro.coinbase.com"
req.url <- "/accounts/"
secret <- "asdf"
api.key <- "1234"
passphrase <- "123"

url <- paste0(api.url, req.url) #"https://api.pro.coinbase.com/accounts/"
timestamp <- format(as.numeric(Sys.time()), digits = 13) # create nonce 
key <- RCurl::base64Decode(secret, mode = "raw") # encode api secret 
method <- "GET" 
what <- paste0(timestamp, method, req.url) # get method 

#create encoded signature----
sign <- RCurl::base64Encode(digest::hmac(key, what, algo = "sha256", raw = TRUE)) # hash 

httpheader <- c(
    'CB-ACCESS-KEY' = api.key,
    'CB-ACCESS-SIGN' = sign,
    'CB-ACCESS-TIMESTAMP' = timestamp,
    'CB-ACCESS-PASSPHRASE' = passphrase,
    'Content-Type' = 'application/json'
  ) 

# Generating GET results
response <- httr::content(httr::GET(url, httr::add_headers(httpheader))) 

```

title: `req_body_raw` blocks setting the Content-Type header
description:
**NOTE**: LOW PRIORITY

I could have this wrong, and/or this could be intended behaviour.

In trying to send a top-level empty list (see https://github.com/r-lib/httr2/issues/115), I figured I could create the required JSON myself and use `req_body_raw`. I didn't see at first that this function takes a type, and I first set the header, that is:

```r
library(httr2)

url <- "http://httpbin.org/"
req <- request(url)

body <- req |>
    req_body_raw("{\"empty_list\":[]}") |>
    req_headers("Content-Type" = "application/json") |>
    req_dry_run()

#> POST / HTTP/1.1
#> Host: httpbin.org
#> User-Agent: httr2/0.1.1 r-curl/4.3.2 libcurl/7.77.0
#> Accept: */*
#> Accept-Encoding: deflate, gzip
#> Content-Length: 17
#> 
#> {"empty_list":[]}
```

But this doesn't set `Content-Type: application/json`. I am a little surprised that the header call coming after the body doesn't "win" the header battle.

This also isn't resolved by setting the header before the `req_body_raw` call (or by setting both).

As expected, all works if the `type` parameter of `req_body_raw` is used instead of setting the header:

```R
library(httr2)

url <- "http://httpbin.org/"
req <- request(url)

body <- req |>
    req_body_raw("{\"empty_list\":[]}", type = "application/json") |>
    req_dry_run()
#> POST / HTTP/1.1
#> Host: httpbin.org
#> User-Agent: httr2/0.1.1 r-curl/4.3.2 libcurl/7.77.0
#> Accept: */*
#> Accept-Encoding: deflate, gzip
#> Content-Type: application/json
#> Content-Length: 17
#> 
#> {"empty_list":[]}
```

title: Formatting of numbers when processed by `req_url_query()`
description:
Not really a bug.


But, I think that some sort of admonition in the documentation on how numbers are converted to text when processed by `req_url_query()` would help prevent surprises as the one below. The first request works, the second does not.

``` r
library(httr2)

start <- 100000

start_int <- as.integer(start)
httr2::request('https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/summary-statistics/api') %>%
  httr2::req_url_path_append('associations') %>%
  httr2::req_url_query(start = start_int, size = 1)
#> <httr2_request>
#> GET
#> https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/summary-statistics/api/associations?start=100000&size=1
#> Body: empty
start_dbl <- as.double(start)
httr2::request('https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/summary-statistics/api') %>%
  httr2::req_url_path_append('associations') %>%
  httr2::req_url_query(start = start_dbl, size = 1)
#> <httr2_request>
#> GET
#> https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/summary-statistics/api/associations?start=1e%2B05&size=1
#> Body: empty
```

Or perhaps an extra argument to `req_url_query()` to control this behaviour?

title: Should printing a httr2_token also redact the ID token?
description:
Contacting an OAuth endpoint will return an `id_token` string if you want to authenticate via [OpenID Connect](https://openid.net/connect/), as well as authorise access. All the major providers support it.
```
r$> tok$credentials

token_type: Bearer      
access_token: <REDACTED>
expires_at: 2021-10-04 09:35:02
refresh_token: <REDACTED>      
scope: https://management.azure.com/user_impersonation https://management.azure.com/.default
ext_expires_in: 3598
id_token:
eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJS......   <-- exposed
expires_on: 1633300507
```
Relevant line in `print.httr2_token`, should probably include `id_token` in the list:

title: HTTP state handler / HTTP event handler
description:
**Discussion/Idea**

For the the interpretation of robots.txt files it turns out that a lot of the interpretation depends on the status of the HTTP-request: server error, client error, returning a robots.txt file or some other format, ...

I put some effort into designing a callback / event handler system. It will do but its all but elegant. 

- https://github.com/ropensci/robotstxt/blob/master/R/rt_request_handler.R
- https://github.com/ropensci/robotstxt/blob/master/R/rt_request_handler_defaults.R


**The question is, if handling different states/events and status messages is a broad enough problem to maybe get handled in httr(2) in a better thought through, consistent and robust manner.**



States and events I have got to handle (just to give an idea of the problem space):

- 404
- client error other than 404
- 5xx (aka server error)
- mime type is not "text/plain"
- response data looks like HTML, XML or JSON (aka it does not look like plain text)
- redirects without domain change
- redirect to subdomain www
- redirects with domain change

title: httr2
description:
httr is a library for two main tasks: creating http requests and parsing the responses. Currently this dichotomoy is a little muddled because:
- There is no explicit request object - it is only created internally by
  the request functions. This tends to lead to large request functions that
  have many arguments passed in ...
- There's no consistent naming scheme that indicates whether a function
  works with a request or a response. This is particuarly confusing for
  functions like `content_type()`: does it set the content type of
  the request or extract the content type of the response?

Additionally, httr was designed prior to the pipe and so uses ... rather than functions that modify an object. This makes the API feel rather different to similar APIs (e.g. rvest). It also makes it harder to test, because you can only easily test the result of issuing a request, not the internal request object. Overall the API feels a little dated, and a little underdesigned.
## Request API
### Basics

``` r
req("http://url.com/") %>% req_fetch()

# req_fetch could be a generic so you could still do
req_fetch("http://url.com/")
```
### Performing the request

The HTTP method doesn't affect the input arguments or the output type, so that suggests that the key API verb should be the output, rather than the HTTP method:

``` r
req("http://url.com") %>% req_fetch()
req("http://url.com") %>% req_async()
req("http://url.com") %>% req_save(path = path)
req("http://url.com") %>% req_stream(fun = fun)
```

The request verb would default to GET, unless a body was set, in which case it would change to POST. Otherwise, you could override yourself in two ways:

``` r
req("http://url.com") %>% req_method("DELETE") %>% req_fetch()
req("http://url.com") %>% req_fetch("DELETE")
```

The first form would be most useful when generating partial requests for API wrappers.
### Url

``` r
# Would generally make smaller functions that took multiple arguments
# This would make iterative url construction much nicer for APIs
req("http://url.com/") %>% 
  req_path("a", username, "b") %>%  # replaces
  req_path_suffix("y") %>%  # appends
  req_path_prefix("x") %>%  # for completeness
  req_query(y = 1) %>% 
  req_params() %>% 
  req_fetch()

# req would need to parse the url so you could start with
req("http://url.com/api/v1/?q=2")

```
### Body

``` r
# This would also lead to a nicer API for bodies
req("http://url.com/") %>% 
  req_body_json(a = 1, b = 2, c = 3) %>% 
  req_fetch() 

# Setting body would change default request type, but you could
# override
req("http://url.com/") %>% 
  req_body_json(a = 1, b = 2, c = 3) %>% 
  req_fetch("PUT") 

req("http://url.com/") %>% 
  req_body_json(a = 1, b = 2, c = 3) %>% 
  req_save(path = "~/Desktop/bigfile.blah") 
  # If path is directory, automatically add name from url?

# req_body_file()
# req_body_form()
# req_body_json()
# req_body_multipart()
# req_body_raw()
```
### Authentication

``` r
req("http://url.com/") %>% req_auth_basic()
req("http://url.com/") %>% req_auth_oauth1()
req("http://url.com/") %>% req_auth_oauth2()
```
### Headers

``` r
req("http://url.com/") %>% 
  req_header(`Content-type` = "application/json") %>% 
  req_header(a_list_from_somewhere_else) # would unlist() inputs as needed.
# list(...) %>% flatten() %>% map_chr(as.character())
```
### Curl

``` r
# And there would be a new function for setting specific curl requests
# These would be applied after other request parameters
req_config()
```
## Response API
### Basics

``` r
resp <- req("http://google.com") %>% req_fetch()

# Pipeable API to check that the response is what you expect
resp %>% 
  resp_check_ok() %>% 
  resp_check_body_xml() %>% 
  resp_content_xml()

# Other functions extract headers
resp %>% resp_headers()
resp %>% resp_content_type()

# And other http components
resp %>% resp_status()
resp %>% resp_url()
resp %>% resp_timings()
```
### Content

``` r
resp %>% resp_content_raw()
resp %>% resp_content_text(encoding = "UTF-8")

# Would rely on user to check content type using helper from above
resp %>% resp_content_json()
resp %>% resp_content_xml()
resp %>% resp_content_html()
resp %>% resp_content_png()
resp %>% resp_content_jpeg()
```

Would not have `resp_content_auto()` because I think time has shown that this is a bad idea.
## New package?

Should be a new package, httr2?

Pros:
- Can start from scratch without having to work with existing API
- Could aim for high unit test coverage from the beginning.
- Documentation will be less confusing because it doesn't have to describe 
  two APIs.

Cons:
- May re-introduce bugs because I miss important logic
- Will have to maintain two packages in the short term (in the long term
  would deprecate httr).

I think the pros probably outweigh the cons - the API will a sufficiently large change that it's worth starting from scratch.

@craigcitro, @jeroenooms, @jennybc I'd love your thoughts on this, if you have a little spare time.

title: serialize NULL as null for JSON
description:
In httr2, PUT/POST/PATCH with a JSON body should turn a NULL field into a JSON null, not an empty object. The current behaviour makes it unnecessarily hard to interface with REST APIs that distinguish between nulls and empty objects.

This is arguably a wart in `jsonlite::toJSON`, but changing that or httr now would probably break too much code. Since httr2 will be a new package, there shouldn't be any legacy issues.

```r
# current behaviour, as seen in httr:::body_config
jsonlite::toJSON(list(a=1, b=list(), c=list(x=2, y=NULL)), auto_unbox=TRUE)
# {"a":1,"b":[],"c":{"x":2,"y":{}}}

# better behaviour
jsonlite::toJSON(list(a=1, b=list(), c=list(x=2, y=NULL)), auto_unbox=TRUE, null="null")
# {"a":1,"b":[],"c":{"x":2,"y":null}}
```

title: OAuth as a new package?
description:
@jennybc  and I discussed this just a bit in DM's - she suggested opening an issue here. 

The major feature `crul` does not have that `httr` does have is OAuth. It's not a common use case in scientific web resources, so there's not a big push for me to support it. However, it would be great if there was an easy way for `crul` users to incorporate OAuth with a separate package. 

There's only two higher level http libraries now, but surely more http libraries will come along in the future, and maybe they'll even be httr and httr2 co-existing. 

Breaking out OAuth into a separate library that could be integrated into any http library seems to make sense. In python theres https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib and ruby has https://github.com/oauth-xx/oauth2 (i may be missing some other libs that are more widely used)

From what Jenny tells me, OAuth in httr is pretty integrated into the package, so maybe it isn't that easy to do?
